claims.text: Traditional analytical predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr generally assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Defect-free analytical predictions have limited accuracy and overestimate HfNbTaTiZr conductivity, particularly at low temperatures.
Explicitly incorporating defects and oxygen-impurity effects will improve conductivity predictions in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The bulk alloy is manufactured by arc melting and homogenized to produce an evenly distributed microstructure.
The nominally oxygen-free specimen contains processing defects such as dislocations and grain boundaries.
A second HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
A 1 wt.% oxygen addition represents a common impurity level.
The proposed model combines atomistic simulations with machine-learning corrections for real defect structures and oxygen-impurity scattering.
Electron-defect scattering dominates conductivity behavior over 0–200 K.
Phonon-induced scattering and defect interactions are relevant over 300–1200 K.
Grain boundaries, dislocations, and oxygen impurities act as electron-scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
These defects and impurities reduce the effective mean free path of charge carriers.
At low temperature, enhanced defect and impurity scattering reduces conductivity relative to perfect-crystal predictions.
At high temperature, coupling between phonon scattering and defect scattering causes conductivity to deviate from simple analytical predictions.
The proposed model will predict a downward conductivity shift over 0–200 K relative to conventional analytical predictions.
The proposed model will predict a more gradual conductivity decline or a modified temperature coefficient over 300–1200 K.
The approach is applicable to bulk high-entropy alloys with similar processing histories and oxygen levels up to 1 wt.%.
The hypothesis is falsified if the advanced model does not reduce conductivity-prediction error by at least 20% relative to the analytical baseline in either temperature regime.
The hypothesis is also falsified if the model predicts the wrong direction of the low-temperature conductivity change.
